item.text: {"text":"Sampled softmax provides competition against multiple negatives and naturally concentrates gradients on high-scoring mistakes; temperature controls this emphasis, with overly aggressive settings risking domination by a few difficult negatives. The 2024 [sampled-softmax analysis](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf) supports ranking benefits but does not establish gains for NextItNet on Electronics. A separate [2024 sequential-recommendation comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276), covering random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling, found dataset-dependent tradeoffs: uniform sampling favored head items, while popularity-based sampling could improve balance at lower overall accuracy. [R²NS, WWW 2026](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) reports that introducing hard negatives too early can underperform uniform sampling; uniform warm-up followed by progressively harder, stochastic selection improves robustness.\n\nFalse-negative safeguards matter because high-scoring unobserved items may be genuine future positives. [EMM, 2026](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026004090) combines hard/random negatives with ID exclusion and similarity-window filtering, although its evidence concerns graph contrastive recommendation rather than NextItNet. Practical hypothesis for this task: retain one NextItNet per category; compare uniform multi-negative sampled softmax against uniform warm-up followed by a modest hard/uniform mixture. Exclude padding, targets and known training positives; sample stochastically among difficult candidates rather than always choosing the maximum. Treat similarity filtering as an ablation, since it can remove useful distinctions. Select temperature, negative count and mixture strength using the fixed four-category macro validation HR@10; inspect Electronics separately without replacing the macro objective. Larger training margins alone provide no evidence of ranking generalization."}
